A few dozen paces inward he found the remains of a man.
Only bones remained, picked clean long ago. Beside the skeleton rested a small hand axe whose wooden haft had long since rotted away.
Visenor crouched.
"I'm sorry."
There was no one left to hear the words.
He recovered the axe head before continuing deeper.
A sudden shadow crossed the cave entrance.
He froze.
Goat.
Only the goat.
Its silhouette lingered for several seconds before disappearing again.
Visenor waited nearly half an hour before moving once more.
No dragon.
No tracks.
No eggs.
Nothing.
Eventually he emerged from the cave and continued climbing.
The terrain grew steeper still.
Ten minutes of climbing left his lungs burning.
Then...
A smell.
Burnt flesh.
Fresh.
He slowed immediately.
Just ahead lay the blackened corpse of a mountain goat.
The hide had been scorched nearly to ash.
Dragonfire.
His heartbeat quickened.
Not far beyond the carcass stood another cave.
This one was larger.
Massive fallen stones framed its entrance.
Visenor remained hidden behind a ridge for several minutes, studying every shadow.
Nothing emerged.
No movement.
No sound.
At last he lit another torch.
Slowly...
Very slowly...
...he entered.
The cavern stretched farther than he expected.
His footsteps echoed softly.
Then he saw it.
Far within the darkness rested a dragon egg.
Visenor stopped breathing.
It truly exists.
His eyes swept across the chamber.
No dragon.
No—
A low rumble rolled through the cave.
Not thunder.
Breathing.
He backed away one careful step.
Another.
His shoulder brushed against stone.
Stone...
...that exhaled.
Visenor's blood turned cold.
The rock moved.
No.
Not rock.
Two enormous folded wings.
They unfolded with startling speed.
Dust cascaded from ancient scales as the creature rose from where it had concealed itself against the cavern wall.
A lean dragon.
Its scales shimmered with pale yellow touched by old bone.
Its eyes fixed upon him.
A growl filled the cave.
Visenor did not reach for his sword.
Instead he spoke.
"Rytsas."
Friend.
The dragon did not answer.
Its growl deepened.
Slowly—carefully—Visenor removed his sword belt.
The blade clattered softly onto the cave floor.
"Rytsas."
The dragon exploded into motion.
One heartbeat it stood across the cavern.
The next it was only a few feet away.
Its wings spread wide.
Its jaws parted.
Heat washed across Visenor's face.
Every instinct screamed at him to run.
He did not.
He forced himself to remain still.
"I will not harm you," he whispered in High Valyrian. "Rytsas."
The dragon hesitated.
For one impossible moment...
...it listened.
Then the scales along its throat began to glow.
Orange.
Brighter.
Brighter still.
The entire cavern flickered beneath the growing light.
Visenor swallowed.
"...Boneskin."
The name escaped him almost without thought.
"Wait."
The dragon lowered its head.
Not in surrender.
In warning.
With a sudden shove of its snout, it struck Visenor square in the chest.
He was thrown backward, tumbling across the stone until he landed outside the cave entrance.
Pain shot through his ribs.
The dragon followed only as far as the mouth of the cavern.
No farther.
Visenor slowly rose, keeping his empty hands visible.
"I did not come to command you," he called in High Valyrian. "I only wish to camp nearby. I mean you no harm. I even left my sword behind."
The dragon regarded him in silence.
Then, without another sound...
...it turned.
Folded its wings.
And vanished once more into the darkness.
Visenor stood there for a long while before allowing himself to breathe again.
That evening he built his camp within sight of the cave.
He did not attempt to enter again.
The journey had taken him deep into the jagged heart of the Red Mountains, a three-day ride followed by two days of agonizing, breathless climbing.
And now, he simply had to wait.
When the mountain winds grew quiet, he sang old Valyrian songs into the night—not loudly, nor as commands, but as one traveler might sing to another beside a lonely fire.
Whether Boneskin listened...
Only the dragon knew.
The bells of King's Landing rang just after sunrise, though they carried little joy these days.

Smoke still drifted above countless chimneys, and the streets below the Red Keep stirred with merchants, gold cloaks, beggars, and hungry mouths. Overhead, dragons wheeled through the pale morning sky, fed well by the Crown and growing larger with every passing moon. One in particular flew lower than the others, banking sharply before unleashing a jet of flame at some unfortunate flock of gulls that had wandered too close to the city walls.
Gaelor watched with quiet satisfaction.

His own dragon had always possessed a savage temper. It burned beetles, birds, and anything else that dared to move before it, yet around its rider it behaved with remarkable obedience, as though violence was simply another form of affection.
"A spirited beast," Saathos observed beside him.
"A dragon should be spirited."
"It reminds me of its master."
Gaelor smirked.
"I'll choose to take that as praise."
Saathos returned no smile. He stepped closer instead, lowering his voice.
"A raven arrived before dawn. I heard the news before it reached the king."
Gaelor's expression hardened.
"What is it?"
"They've found Ser Curtass Whent."
Gaelor frowned immediately.
"...Alive?"
"No."
The answer came without hesitation.
"They found six bodies in the forest. Ser Curtass among them."
Silence lingered between them.
Gaelor folded his arms.
"Six men..." he repeated. "Were they killed by men, or did they stumble across some great beast? Curtass was no easy knight to bring down."
"Sword wounds," Saathos replied. "Every one of them."
"And Whent?"
A brief pause.
"The reports say his face was ruined beyond recognition. Whatever happened to the others... something else happened to him."
Gaelor looked toward the city below, thoughtful now.
"Go on."
"The men searching the area found no village, no camp, nothing worth noting. The only place within an hour or so was a sept."
"They searched it?"
"They did."
"And?"
"The septons knew nothing—or claimed to know nothing. No one spoke." Saathos glanced toward the courtyard. "There was, however, a traveler lodging there that night."
Gaelor's eyes narrowed.
"What did he see?"
"Very little. He recalled hearing horses around the same time Ser Curtass is believed to have died. He also remembered a knight stopping briefly at the sept."
"Only one?"
"So he claims."
Gaelor exhaled slowly.
"A single knight..."
"Whether that knight matters or not remains to be seen."
"It rarely means nothing."
Before either man could say more, the bells sounded again.
Not alarm bells.
Welcome bells.
Both men turned toward the castle gates.
A column of riders entered the outer yard beneath fluttering banners of House Dayne.
Saathos smiled first.
"It seems Ser Alester has returned."
Gaelor watched the convoy climb toward the keep.
"...Alive."
"For now."
"For now," Gaelor echoed.
Then he descended the steps to greet them.
Lady Lorenah Dayne pulled back her hood before the horses had fully stopped.
The journey south had left dust upon her cloak and weariness beneath her violet eyes, but neither diminished the effortless grace with which she dismounted.
Jace was already waiting.
"It is good to see you again, my lady."
"It was an exhausting road, Prince Jace."
Her voice carried the soft music of Dorne.
Jace smiled.
"I trust you managed to keep my knight safe."
A faint grin tugged at Lorenah's lips.
"Should you not be asking whether he managed to keep us safe?"
Behind her, Ser Alester allowed himself the smallest of smiles.
Jace laughed.
"I stand corrected."
Lorenah looked around the castle yard.
"It has been many years since I last came to King's Landing."
More than a few curious eyes had settled upon her.
"They're staring," she observed.
"They're staring because you're a Dayne."
"I doubt that."
"You give the city too much credit."
She glanced toward the crowded streets below Aegon's High Hill.
"The roads were full of hungry people. We distributed what food we could spare before reaching the castle."
Jace's smile faded.
"We are living through unhappy days."
"So I gathered."
"And my brothers have done precious little to improve them."
Lorenah nodded once.
"If you'll forgive me, I'd like a proper bath before supper."
"Of course."
She departed with her attendants.
Jace remained where he stood until she disappeared inside.
Only then did he turn toward the knight climbing stiffly from his horse.
Alester looked considerably worse than when he had left.
Bruises still colored his face.
Several fresh scars disappeared beneath his collar.
His movements betrayed pain despite every effort to hide it.
For a long moment neither man spoke.
Then Jace crossed the distance between them and embraced him.
"I haven't slept properly since I sent you away."
Alester chuckled.
"My prince... did you truly doubt me?"
"I trusted you."
Jace pulled back enough to meet his eyes.
"I did not trust the men I knew would be following you."
Alester lowered his head.
"I know."
Then, with a crooked grin—
"I'll try not to make a habit of it."
Jace laughed despite himself.
"See that you don't."
Together they entered the keep, surrendering their horses to the stablemaster before disappearing into the halls of the Red Keep.
By the time Alester had exchanged his travel-worn armor for clean clothes, the servants had withdrawn, leaving the chamber blessedly quiet.
Jace poured wine for them both.
"Well?" Alester asked as he eased himself into a chair. "How fares the capital?"
Jace let out a weary breath.
"Poorly."
"That bad?"
"Worse."
Alester accepted the cup with a grateful nod.
"We heard rumors on the road. About Prince Gaelor."
Jace snorted into his wine.
"He's a bloody fool."
Alester merely smiled into his cup.
"I suppose I'd best keep my thoughts to myself."
"No," Jace said. "Say them."
The knight hesitated only a heartbeat.
"I imagine whatever hopes remained with House Tyrell have died now. I doubt we'll be sharing a hall with them again."
"I doubt it as well."
As Alester lifted his cup, something caught his eye.
Pinned upon Jace's doublet was the brooch of the Hand.
His brows rose.
"...Congratulations, my prince."
Jace followed his gaze before giving a humorless laugh.
"I'm as surprised as you are."
"You've earned it."
"So they say."
"It is a wise decision."
"I suspect it's little more than a title." Jace swirled the wine in his cup. "No one seems particularly interested in listening to the Hand."
"Then why reward you at all?"
Jace smiled thinly.
"If you've figured out my father, I'd dearly love to hear the answer."
Alester laughed.
"No man alive has managed that."
For a time they drank in comfortable silence.
Then Alester's expression darkened.
"Lord Derrin Hightower."
Jace looked up.
"You've heard."
"All this time... he was right in front of our nose."
"He was. Right until the moment he breathed his last at my feet."
Alester stared at him for a moment before quietly refilling both cups.
Jace waved a hand dismissively after telling him about how they uncovered the plot constructed by the Tyrells and the late Hand.
"Enough about King's Landing. Tell me everything."
Alester leaned back carefully.
"How is Princess Saera?"
Jace sighed.
"Not well."
"No?"
"She's... worse than when you left."
Concern crossed Alester's face, though he quickly hid it.
After a pause, he said quietly,
"We encountered Ser Curtass."
Jace's eyes sharpened immediately.
"I did what had to be done."
"What happened?"
"There were six of them."
"Six?"
Alester nodded.
"I had already sent Prince Visenor ahead. The princess was still with us. We couldn't risk both of them."
"You went alone?"
"There wasn't another choice."
Jace stared.
"You fought six men by yourself?"
"For Her Grace's safety." Alester glanced toward the scars still healing beneath his sleeves and gave a small, self-deprecating smile. "In hindsight... perhaps not my finest decision."
Jace shook his head in disbelief.
"Gods... did you truly fight them all alone?"
"I did."
"And lived."
"I've never fought a battle like that before."
His voice remained calm, but Jace noticed the distant look settling into his eyes.
"It was the hardest fight of my life."
"The fact you're sitting here at all is a miracle."
Alester chuckled.
"The gods weren't finished with me."
Jace laughed quietly.
"I suppose not."
"We eventually reached Starfall."
"And?"
"Lady Lorenah already knows."
Jace frowned.
"Knows what?"
"We were discovered."
"So quickly?"
"Her whisperers."
Alester shook his head.
"We hadn't been inside Starfall half an hour before we were found."
Jace leaned back slowly.
"...Impressive."
"I entrusted Prince Visenor to her care."
"I noticed."
"I made certain she understood you sent me there to put Prince Visenor under her protection."
Jace considered that for several moments.
"That was the right decision."
"I hope so."
"We don't know her well."
"We didn't have the luxury of certainty."
Jace nodded reluctantly.
"I suppose we didn't."
Alester looked into his wine.
"I only regret we failed to remain hidden."
"You reached Starfall."
"Barely."
"You completed a journey few men in Westeros could have."
Alester smiled faintly.
"I fear I also embarrassed myself rather spectacularly along the way."
Jace laughed.
"A little."
The knight groaned.
"I thought as much."
"But besides that?" Jace reached over and lightly tapped one of Alester's bruised shoulders. "I'd say you did rather well."
Alester smiled.
Seeing it eased something inside Jace he had not realized he had been carrying.
"How are Prince Visenor and Princess Rhaella?" he asked.
"They've settled in well."
"They're safe?"
"They're safe."
Jace released a breath he hadn't known he was holding.
"Good."
A thoughtful silence followed before Jace spoke again.
"We'll need a way to communicate."
Alester frowned.
"I actually thought the opposite."
"No contact at all?"
"The less correspondence between Starfall and King's Landing, the better."
"Perhaps."
Jace looked toward the window overlooking the city.
"But sooner or later we'll have no choice."
Alester nodded.
"I imagine that discussion now belongs to you... and Lady Lorenah."
"I imagine it does."
For a moment neither man spoke.
Then Jace lifted his cup.
"May the gods look kindly upon us."
Alester raised his own.
"We'll need them to."
After another drink, Jace set his cup aside and stood.
"You've earned your rest."
"My prince—"
"That's an order."
Alester smiled.
"...As you command."
Jace left him alone to sleep, though as the door closed behind him, he found himself wondering whether either of them truly believed the hardest days were behind them.
The sun had begun its slow descent when Jace found Lady Lorenah strolling through the gardens overlooking Blackwater Bay.

She had exchanged the dust of the road for a gown of pale lavender, though there remained something unmistakably Dornish in the ease with which she carried herself. The gardens of the Red Keep were carefully tended, every hedge trimmed and every flower placed with purpose. Beautiful, certainly—but ordered.
Too ordered.
"You seem well rested," Jace said as he approached.
"I am."
She turned toward him with a small smile.
"The castle is beautiful."
"I'll happily take that as a compliment."
"The castle is." Her eyes wandered toward the towering walls surrounding them. "The city beyond them... less so."
Jace laughed softly.
"I can't argue."
"It's all rather formal."
"It tends to be."
"I think I preferred the streets."
"The streets?"
"I've heard stories of Flea Bottom."
Jace blinked.
"...You have?"
"They say it's unlike anywhere else in Westeros."
"It is."
"Then we should go."
He looked at her as though she had suggested a stroll beyond the Wall.
"My lady..."
"No."
She smiled mischievously.
"If we're going, you'll stop calling me that."
"I beg your pardon?"
"We're hardly going to blend in if you keep addressing me as my lady every other sentence."
Jace rubbed the back of his neck.
"Fair point."
"I've always wanted to see it."
"You've also always wanted to survive it, I hope."
"They say it's... exotic."
"They also say many people are robbed there before sunset."
"Only many?"
"On a quiet day."
She laughed.
"I still wish to see it."
Jace's amusement faded.
"The timing couldn't be worse."
She tilted her head.
"My brother has given the smallfolk every reason to resent this family."
"I've heard."
"They're angry. Rightfully so."
For a heartbeat neither spoke.
Then Lorenah reached into the folds of her cloak.
"I almost forgot."
She unfolded a length of finely woven black cloth embroidered with silver Dornish patterns.
"I brought you something."
Jace accepted it carefully.
The workmanship was exquisite.
"This is beautiful."
"I thought black suited you."
"It does now."
She raised an eyebrow, glancing knowingly toward his newly darkened hair.
"It certainly does."
He smiled despite himself.
"If we truly mean to disappear into Flea Bottom..."
"...then perhaps neither of us should be dressed like nobility."
"I was about to suggest the same."
"We'll need rags."
"I never imagined I'd hear a Dayne ask for rags."
"I never imagined I'd ask."
They both laughed.
"So," she said, turning toward the castle.
"Shall we?"
Jace folded the shawl over one arm.
"I know a place that serves tolerable fish."
"Tolerable?"
"In Flea Bottom that's practically a royal feast."
She grinned.
"Lead the way."
Together they walked back toward the keep to prepare, leaving behind the carefully trimmed gardens for a city that smelled of smoke, salt, mud, and life.
Far above them, dragons circled lazily over King's Landing, their shadows drifting across the towers like passing clouds.
That same afternoon, another corner of the Red Keep was filled not with politics or whispered reports, but with tears.
Naella hurried through the corridors with scarcely a thought for courtly decorum. The moment she caught sight of Gaelor, she broke into a run.
"My prince!"
Before he could ask what had happened, she had thrown her arms around him.
He caught her instinctively.
"Naella?"
She pulled back just enough for him to see the tears glistening in her eyes—not tears of grief.
"My prince..." she whispered, smiling through them. "I'm with child."
Gaelor simply stared.
For a heartbeat, it was as though he had forgotten how to speak.
"...Are you serious?"
She laughed softly, nodding.
"Your seed is strong... just like you."
A broad grin spread across his face before he kissed her.
The noise of the castle seemed to vanish around them.
When they finally parted, Gaelor rested both hands upon her shoulders.
"This..." He laughed in disbelief. "This is wonderful."
"It is."
"We must tell the king."
"Immediately."
"In times like these..." His smile only widened. "This may be the best news Father's heard in months."
Still hand in hand, they made for the king's solar.
The guards outside moved to stop them.
"His Grace is occupied."
"It cannot wait."
The guards exchanged uncertain looks before reluctantly allowing them through.
Inside, King Baelenys was already listening to a messenger.
The king lifted one hand as Gaelor entered.
"Wait."
Gaelor obeyed.
The messenger continued.
"...our search led us to a nearby sept, Your Grace. The men stationed there knew little, though one traveler claimed a knight had stopped there shortly before your man was attacked."
Baelenys looked almost bored.
"So."
The messenger hesitated.
"Ser Curtass Whent is dead, Your Grace."
"Yes."
Another pause.
"It appears he died carrying out the task you assigned him."
Baelenys shrugged.
"He knew the risks."
No anger.
No surprise.
Only indifference.
"He died doing his duty. See that the proper honors are given to him and be done with it."
The messenger shifted uneasily.
"Your Grace... perhaps there is still value in learning who—"
"I've heard enough."
Silence swallowed the chamber.
Then Baelor, who had remained quiet until now, finally spoke.
"Send someone to that sept. If Whent died for something, we might as well discover what."
Gaelor intervened.
"Saathos should go."
"He is reliable."
Baelor considered for only a moment.
"Very well."
He looked back to the messenger.
"Send Ser Saathos."
The man bowed deeply before withdrawing.
The door closed.
Only then did Gaelor's excitement return.
"Father..."
Baelenys looked toward him.
"I've better news."
Naella stepped forward.
"I'm with child."
For the first time since entering the room, surprise touched the king's face.
His eyes settled upon Naella.
Then, with unexpected gentleness, he reached out and patted her cheek.
A small gesture.
An awkward one.
Yet sincere.
He gave Gaelor a single approving nod.
"See that your princess is well cared for."
Another nod.
"Well done."
And just as quickly as the moment had come...
...the king walked past them and left the room.
Gaelor watched him go before looking back to Naella.
She slipped her hand into his once more.
He squeezed it gently.
"Is there anything you need?"
Naella smiled.
"Only one thing."
"Name it."
"I need you to be happy."
His smile softened.
"And stop letting your brother trouble your heart."
For once...
Gaelor found he had no answer.
The disguise suited neither of them.
Lorenah insisted it was perfect.
Jace insisted it was dreadful.

She had wrapped a faded shawl around her head until only her violet eyes remained visible. Jace wore a coarse hood over his silver hair, his clothes exchanged for worn wool and patched linen borrowed from castle servants. No prince had ever looked quite so uncomfortable trying to resemble a common laborer.
"You still walk like someone who's never carried a bucket in his life," Lorenah observed.
"I have carried buckets."
"When?"
Jace thought for a moment.
"...You've found me out."
She laughed.

By the time they descended into Flea Bottom, the evening streets had begun to swell with life. Musicians played battered fiddles outside alehouses while children darted through muddy alleys with impossible speed. Hawkers shouted over one another, selling everything from roasted onions to chipped daggers, old boots, and charms promising fortune or fertility.
The smell was another matter entirely.
Smoke, fish, stale ale, sweat, damp timber, and humanity blended into something uniquely King's Landing.
Lorenah slowed almost immediately.
"Oh, this is marvelous."
"Marvelous?"
"It feels... alive."
Jace smiled despite himself.
"You may be the only noblewoman in Westeros to say that."
A fire breather had gathered a small crowd near an alley mouth. He swallowed another mouthful of oil before sending a great plume of flame roaring into the twilight.
Lorenah leaned forward with delighted laughter.
"Now that would never be allowed at court."
"No," Jace admitted. "It wouldn't."
A little farther along, an elderly woman sat behind a rough wooden table covered in polished stones of every imaginable color.
"Magic gems!" she cried. "Lucky gems! Gems blessed by the Seven!"
Lorenah crouched beside the table.
"Do you suppose they're truly enchanted?"
Jace folded his arms.
"They will be the moment you wear one."
She looked back at him with mock disapproval.
"And my lady will not be buying anything."
"My—"
"We're in Flea Bottom."
"Right."
"No titles."
Jace nodded solemnly.
"Very well... Lorenah."
She clicked her tongue.
"Still too noble."
"What would you have me call you?"
She considered.
"...Not Lorenah."
"Helpful."
"You need another name."
"So do you."
She looked him up and down thoughtfully.
"You look like a Derrick."
"Derrick?"
"It suits you."
Jace sighed.
"Then I'll call you Dany."
She stared at him for a heartbeat before bursting into laughter.
"You've lost your wits."
"I wasn't aware I'd ever possessed them."
"I believe King's Landing has finally driven you mad."
"I've lived here long enough."
They continued deeper into the district until Jace stopped outside a narrow alehouse.
"The fish isn't terrible."
"That glowing recommendation again."
"In Flea Bottom that's practically a royal feast."
She grinned.
"Lead the way."
Inside, the benches were crowded and the air thick with laughter and spilled ale.
They were served a pair of rough wooden bowls filled with fish stew, dark bread, and cheap ale.
No cutlery arrived.
Lorenah looked around.
"...With their hands?"
"With their hands."
She shrugged.
"When in Flea Bottom."
A moment later they were both eating like everyone else.
Some broth found its way onto Lorenah's cheek.
Without thinking, Jace reached across the table and brushed it away with his thumb.
Neither spoke for a heartbeat.
Then a small body collided gently with Lorenah's shoulder.
A boy—perhaps eight years old—froze where he stood.
His eyes widened.
Not because he recognized her.
Because of her eyes.
He had never seen eyes that color before.
Lorenah smiled warmly.
"And what's your name?"
The boy mumbled something too quietly for Jace to catch.
"I'm Dany," she replied with a playful smile before taking the child's hand. "Shall I read your fortune?"
The boy nodded eagerly.
She studied his tiny palm with exaggerated seriousness.
She traced one line with a finger.
"I think..."
The child leaned closer.
"...we'll meet again someday."
His face lit with delight.
He fumbled at his pocket, clearly searching for a coin.
Finding none, he looked down in embarrassment.
Lorenah closed his fingers gently.
"No payment."
She smiled.
"Keep it."
The boy beamed before disappearing back into the crowd.
Lorenah watched him go.
"I ought to come here more often."
Jace laughed.
"There is nothing like this in Starfall."
"There isn't?"
"Dorne has places with life..." she said, looking around the crowded room. "But Starfall is peaceful."
She smiled to herself.
"Almost too peaceful."
Jace raised his cup.
"You'd always be welcome."
She lifted hers in return.
"I shall remember that."
They wandered long after the meal was finished.

The crowds thinned as the hour grew later, leaving behind quieter lanes where the noise of taverns became a distant murmur and lantern light spilled across uneven cobblestones. Here and there, voices drifted from open windows, mingling with the strains of some old song carried on the evening breeze.
Lorenah walked a step ahead, her shawl still concealing all but her eyes.
"So," she said at last, slowing her pace. "Tell me something."
"I'm listening."
"Why did you send your brother to me?"
Jace looked at her.
"And why," she continued, "did you trust me in particular?"
He was silent for a moment.
"You made quite an impression the day we met."
She smiled to herself.
"I've always believed first impressions matter."
"They do."
"So you saw something in me."
"I did."
She glanced sideways.
"What was it?"
Jace chuckled softly.
"No one speaks to a Targaryen prince the way you do."
"No?"
"No."
"That hardly sounds wise."
"It isn't."
He smiled.
"Which is precisely why it stood out."
Lorenah laughed quietly.
"Or perhaps Ser Alester Dayne is simply a very clever man."
"He is."
"The moment he arrived in Dorne, he became... nervous."
"Nervous?"
"He avoided my eyes. Chose his words too carefully." She looked toward him knowingly. "It made me wonder."
Jace remained silent.
"So I asked myself a question."
She stopped walking.
"Did Prince Jace truly intend to entrust his brother to me..."
"...or did Ser Alester simply have the misfortune of being discovered the moment he crossed into Dorne?"
Jace met her gaze.
"You've already read my fortune."
"No."
"I think you have."
She smiled faintly.
"I merely pay attention."
After a brief silence she continued.
"You needn't worry."
"About?"
"No word of your brother will leave Starfall."
"I believed that from the beginning."
"Did you?"
"I did."
He hesitated.
"But I still wonder."
"What?"
"Why?"
She tilted her head.
"Why help us?"
"Yes."
Lorenah looked up at the stars beginning to appear overhead.
"Perhaps I'm simply kind."
"I don't believe that."
She laughed.
"Nor should you."
"I'm a Dornishwoman."
"And I'm a Targaryen."
"Our kingdoms have shed enough blood to drown rivers."
"They have."
"By every measure..." she said quietly, "I ought to be your enemy."
Jace smiled.
"I rather thought I already was."
That drew another laugh from her.
"Perhaps," she said after a moment, "we could be the ones to end that."
"The ones to make peace?"
"Why not?"
Jace looked toward the lights stretching across King's Landing.
"Peace wouldn't be the worst thing to happen to this realm."
"No."
She stepped closer until they stood side by side beneath the open sky.
"We breathe the same air."
She looked upward.
"We stand beneath the same stars."
Her voice softened.
"Why must we always find reasons to hate one another?"
Jace's smile faded.
"I wish my father asked himself the same question."
"He doesn't?"
"The only language he truly understands is conquest."
"And you?"
"I've earned something of a reputation."
"What sort?"
He laughed under his breath.
"For disagreeing."
Lorenah regarded him for a long moment before humming a quiet Dornish melody as they resumed walking.
Eventually she asked,
"How long do you intend for me to remain in King's Landing?"
"I had hoped..." Jace said carefully, "...that once things settled somewhat, we might hold a tourney."
"A tourney?"
He nodded.
"It would do the city some good."
"And if the Prince competes?"
Jace grinned.
"Do you think Prince Gaelor could resist?"
"I've heard enough about him to doubt it."
"And you?"
She looked at him over her shoulder.
"If our prince rides..."
"I shall, if I could have your favor."
"Then perhaps I ought to stay."
"I was hoping you'd say that."
She smiled.
"Very well."
"It's settled."
By the time they reached the castle gates, the city had fallen quiet beneath the night.
Jace escorted her to the chambers prepared for House Dayne.
At her door, Lorenah paused.
"I've never had an evening quite like this."
"You've never wandered Flea Bottom in disguise?"
"I should hope not."
He laughed.
"No... neither had I."
"You've lived here all these years."
"I've visited."
"But never like this."
"Never."
She stepped closer.
"Then perhaps," she said softly, "we've both gained something tonight."
Before he could answer, she rose onto her toes and placed a light kiss at the corner of his mouth.
"Until morning, Derrick."
Then she slipped inside, leaving him standing speechless in the corridor.
For several heartbeats, he simply stared at the closed door.
Only then did the smile spread across his face.
He had scarcely gone a dozen paces before another familiar voice interrupted his thoughts.
"You look happy."
Princess Saera stood beneath the torchlight, studying him with quiet amusement.
"Lady Dayne has arrived."
"I noticed."
Jace smiled.
"I'm happier to see you."
Saera rolled her eyes.
"So charming."
"Alester returned as well."
"I know."
"You haven't gone to see him?"
She raised an eyebrow.
"You expect me to visit him?"
"He's exhausted."
"And if Ser Alester wishes to see the king's daughter," she replied with the faintest smile, "he knows perfectly well where to find her."
With that, she continued down the corridor, leaving Jace chuckling to himself.
He changed direction instead.
There was one knight who deserved waking.
Jace knocked softly.
There was no answer.
He knocked again.
"Ser Alester?"
A weary voice came from within.
"I'm awake."
"You don't sound awake."
"I rarely do."
Jace pushed the door open.
Alester was seated on the edge of the bed, already dressed once more, though his injuries still protested every movement.
"I just ran into Princess Saera."
That was enough to draw the knight's attention.
"Oh?"
"I imagine she'd like to see you."
Alester gave a small, uncertain smile.
"I would have gone."
"But?"
He glanced at the fading bruises across his face in the polished steel mirror.
"I wasn't certain presenting myself like... this... would be appropriate."
Jace laughed.
"So this is what concerns you?"
"It should."
"Who do you think you're fooling?"
Jace leaned casually against the doorframe and continued.
"...Apparently not Lady Dayne."
Alester looked genuinely alarmed.
"Lady Dayne?"
"I explained everything."
Alester's shoulders visibly relaxed.
"I suspected as much."
"She seems trustworthy."
"I believe she is."
Silence settled for a moment before Alester asked,
"And your evening?"
Jace smiled despite himself.
"It went rather well."
"I can see that."
"There is one problem."
"Oh?"
"I need you to teach me jousting."
Alester blinked.
"A tourney."
"There will be one?"
"I intend to ride."
The knight folded his arms.
"My prince..."
"What?"
"You're not a knight."
Jace smiled.
"Not yet."
Alester frowned thoughtfully.
"The Lord Commander believes I'm ready. But what about you?"
"If that is his judgment..."
He nodded slowly.
"...then mine carries little weight."
"I asked for your opinion."
Alester met his eyes.
"I think you're ready."
Jace's grin widened.
"Good."
"Tomorrow morning we could go together and Ser Morrigen can knight you."
"I had another thought."
"What sort of thought?"
Jace stepped into the room and quietly shut the door behind him.
"You could knight me."
Alester stared.
"...I beg your pardon?"
"You heard me."
"My prince..."
"You were my knight."
"I was."
"I practically served as your squire."
"I wouldn't say you served."
"Hey!"
Alester looked genuinely alarmed.
"I cannot simply knight a prince in the middle of his bedchamber."
"Why not?"
"...Because that's absurd."
Jace shrugged.
"I have no need for a gallery of lords or the gaze of the court. To kneel before Ser Alester Dayne is an honor; to be raised by my brother’s hand is the only blessing I require."
Jace had already dropped to one knee.
Alester froze.
For one spectacularly awkward moment...
...he panicked.
Then, entirely on instinct...
...he knelt as well.
Jace looked at him.
Alester looked back.
Several silent heartbeats passed.
Then Jace frowned.
"...Are you an idiot?"
Realization struck Alester all at once.
"Oh."
He immediately climbed back to his feet.
"My apologies."
Jace burst into laughter.
"So much for dignity."
"I appear to have misplaced mine."
Alester drew his sword.
The familiar steel caught the candlelight as he rested its flat gently upon Jace's shoulder.
His expression, moments ago embarrassed, became solemn.
He recited the ancient vows every knight of the Seven Kingdoms knew by heart.
"In the name of the Warrior, I charge you to be brave."
"In the name of the Father, I charge you to be just."
"In the name of the Mother, I charge you to defend the young and innocent."
When the final words had been spoken, he lifted the blade. A faint smile touched his lips.
"Arise, Ser Jacaelon, a knight of the Seven Kingdoms."
Jace stood.
For a moment he could say nothing.
His eyes glistened.
Alester noticed before politely pretending not to.
Instead he simply embraced him.
"Congratulations."
"Thank you."
"You've earned it."
"I hope so."
"You have."
After another quiet moment, Alester sheathed his sword.
"I suppose I should finally visit the princess."
"I believe she'd pretend not to have been waiting."
Alester laughed.
"I believe you're right."
He left the room.
Jace remained behind only long enough to remove his boots before finally lying down, the words Rise, Ser Jacaelon still echoing in his thoughts.
As Alester crossed the silent corridors, a faint glow beneath one door caught his eye.
Candlelight.
He stopped.
Then knocked gently.
"Princess Saera?"
The door opened almost at once.
Saera studied him from head to toe without speaking.
Finally she said,
"...They did quite a number on you."
Alester smiled faintly.
"They did."
"So perhaps my brother exaggerated your invincibility."
"I'm only a knight, Your Grace."
"Just like all the others?"
"Just like all the others."
She folded her arms.
"And yet many knights forget their vows."
Her violet eyes searched his face.
"Do you?"
"Never."
For the first time that evening, she smiled.
"I'm glad you've returned."
A pause.
"...Though perhaps not quite as glad as my brother."
Alester laughed softly.
"Before I left, we used to walk together whenever time allowed."
"We did."
"I wondered..."
He hesitated.
"...if you'd care for another walk."
Saera considered him for several moments.
"I should think about it."
He bowed his head.
"Of course."
Another heartbeat passed.
Then—
"...Very well."
They stepped into the corridor together.
From farther down the gallery, unnoticed behind a stone pillar, Jace watched them disappear into the torchlit halls.

Only after they had vanished from sight did he turn away, wearing the quiet smile of a brother who believed, if only for one evening, that perhaps the gods had shown his family a small measure of mercy.
For two days, the dragon never left his thoughts.

Visenor made no attempt to enter the cave again. Each morning he woke before dawn, tended his fire, and waited. Sometimes he spoke in High Valyrian. Sometimes he sang the old songs of the Freehold, letting the melodies drift through the mountain air without expectation of an answer. Other times he simply sat in silence, content to let the dragon know he had not come as a hunter.
The mountain remained patient.
So did he.
Shortly after sunrise on the seventh day, the silence broke.
Boneskin emerged from the cave.

The dragon threw back its head and loosed a thunderous roar that rolled through the cliffs. Its yellowed scales caught the morning light like old ivory, and smoke curled lazily from its nostrils as it fixed its gaze upon the lone Targaryen who had refused to leave.
Visenor rose slowly.
He kept his hands where the dragon could see them.
"Lykirī," he said calmly. "Rytsas."
Easy. Friend.
Boneskin answered with another low growl.
"I've come to make peace with you," Visenor continued in High Valyrian. "Not to command you."
His voice remained steady, though he stood straighter than before. Not submissive.
Not challenging.
Simply resolute.
"I will not harm you."
He reached into one of his packs and carefully placed strips of dried meat upon a flat stone several paces away before retreating.
Boneskin lowered its head.
It sniffed the offering.
Then, without so much as tasting it, the dragon spread its wings.
With a single powerful beat, it launched itself from the mountainside.
Visenor watched until it became little more than a speck against the pale Dornish sky.
"So much for that."
He almost laughed.
Nearly three quarters of an hour passed before the familiar silhouette returned.
Boneskin descended in a wide circle before landing heavily outside the cave.
Something hung limp from its jaws.
A mountain goat.
Freshly slain.
The carcass landed at Visenor's feet.
He looked from the goat...
...to the dragon.
"...Is this for me?"
Boneskin merely watched.
Visenor drew his knife.
"If that's the case..."
He carved away a piece of meat and ate.
The flesh was still warm.
Moments later, Boneskin stepped forward, tore into the opposite side of the carcass, and began feeding beside him.
Man and dragon shared the same meal.
Neither hurried.
Neither threatened the other.
The only sounds were tearing flesh and the distant cry of hawks circling above the peaks.
When the meal was finished, Visenor wiped his hands upon his cloak and slowly extended one arm.
Boneskin noticed immediately.
A faint rumble escaped the dragon's throat.
Visenor stopped.
He waited.
The rumble faded.
Another careful step.
Another.
He never broke eye contact.
When he was finally close enough, his fingertips brushed the rough, warm scales along the dragon's neck.
Boneskin did nothing.
Visenor rested his palm there.
The scales felt harder than polished stone, yet warm with the heat of the dragon's blood.
Slowly...
Very slowly...
He stroked the creature's neck.
Boneskin remained still.
A smile found its way onto Visenor's face.
"Rytsas," he whispered.
Friend.
He had not climbed these mountains expecting to return astride a dragon.
That had never been the purpose.
He had come seeking proof.
A place.
A beginning.
Now he had all three.
There would be time enough for greater ambitions.
Not today.
Today, friendship was enough.
He remained outside the cave until the afternoon, saying little, allowing the dragon to grow accustomed to his presence. When at last he gathered his belongings, Boneskin watched him in silence.
"I'll return," Visenor promised in High Valyrian.
"I won't forget."
The dragon did not follow.
It simply remained at the cave mouth, its great head tilted ever so slightly as the prince descended the mountain.
Visenor looked back only once.
Boneskin was still watching.
He smiled to himself.
"I'll be back."
This time, the words sounded less like a promise...
...and more like the beginning of one.
Roach greeted him with an indignant snort after nearly four days alone.
"I missed you too."

The old gelding carried him down the remaining trails far more quickly than they had climbed them. By the time the first light of dawn spilled across the Torrentine, the towers of Starfall stood once more against the brightening sky.
Visenor scarcely waited for the stable hands.
He all but leapt from the saddle and hurried through the castle.
Rhaella found him before he found her.
One look at his face was enough.
"You found it."
He laughed.
"I found him."
She embraced him tightly.
"Tell me everything."
He did.

Over cups of Dornish wine that soon became a bottle, he recounted every step of the journey—the burned goat, the hidden cave, the dragon egg, the first terrifying meeting with Boneskin, the songs, the waiting, and finally the meal they had shared together.
Long after the wine had run dry, they remained wrapped in one another's arms.
Outside, dawn bathed Starfall in pale gold.
Inside, for the first time in many years, Visenor allowed himself to believe that fate might yet have reserved something extraordinary for him.

title: Chapter VIII: The Viper in Silk
synopsis: As a grand tourney approaches, Prince Gaelor enacts a brutal punishment to bury a royal scandal. Far to the south, Visenor claims his winged birthright, while a dangerous encounter in Flea Bottom brings Jacaelon face-to-face with a ghost from his family's past.
content: The Third Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC

Prince Gaelor stood by the tall, arched windows of the Red Keep, nursing a goblet of arbor gold. Beside him, Maester Cordin offered a smile so deeply ingrained it seemed carved into his wrinkled face.

"So, Maester," Gaelor said, his tone thick with casual arrogance. "With my great-uncle Baelor returned to the capital, have you found yourself cast out into the cold? Are your days of whispering in the King's ear at an end?"

Cordin dipped his head, his heavy chain clinking softly against his robes. "As our King sees fit, my Prince. A maester serves the realm, not his own pride. Grand Maester Baelor is a man of unparalleled intellect."
Gaelor snorted. "He is an old man who prefers the scent of dusty parchment to the smell of blood."

"Perhaps," Cordin agreed smoothly. "But a prince who means to rule must understand both. Your father's reign, for instance. The smallfolk and the lords whisper the word cruel behind closed doors, but words are wind. They forget the truth of it: fifteen years of unbroken peace. Peace born of terror, yes, but peace nonetheless."
Gaelor took a slow sip. "He knows how to end a war."

"He knows how to end a war before the banners are even called," Cordin corrected, stepping closer. "Take the matter of your uncle, Vahaemon. Your father was the rightful heir once your uncle Malaenar renounced his claim due to his infirmity. But Vahaemon believed the throne should pass to him. He was a mother’s boy, deeply tied to the late Princess Vhaemys. And she... well, they say when the gods tossed her coin, it landed on the wrong side. She was possessed by a quiet madness. Together, they plotted. They deemed your father’s claim unjust."

Cordin lowered his voice, dropping into the cadence of a storyteller. "It bred a cold war within the House of the Dragon. The entire realm held its breath, waiting for the sky to burn in a Targaryen civil war. Vahaemon played the part of the good, gentle prince perfectly. But he was a viper in silk, squeezing every drop of goodwill for his own advantage. Everyone thought the tension would last for years." Cordin smiled thinly. "Your father ended that cold war in the seventh moon of his reign. Decisively."
Gaelor listened, storing the lesson away. A true king does not wait for the viper to strike.

Three floors above, Princess Maela stood by the glass of her chamber window, gazing down into the shadowed gardens. Two figures were strolling along the gravel paths. Ser Alester Dayne and her sister, Saera.
Maela turned away, a restless hum in her blood. "Enter," she called out, hearing the heavy boots of her sworn shield outside her oak door.

Ser Brannyn Vance stepped into the room. He wore the pristine white cloak of the Kingsguard, but beneath it, he was just a man. Maela had already instructed her maids to brew the bitter, foul-tasting moon tea, leaving a steaming cup on her vanity. She was not a fool.
"What is the mood of the castle, Ser Vance?" she asked, unlacing the silken ties of her robe. "What do the whispers say?"
Vance cleared his throat, his eyes darting away from her exposed shoulder before returning, drawn like a moth to a flame. "I am only a sworn shield, Princess. I hear only echoes."
"Let them play their games," Maela murmured, stepping closer, letting the robe slip entirely to the floor. "We shall play ours."

Gaelor walked the dim corridors of the royal apartments, the wine sitting warm and heavy in his belly. As he passed Maela’s chambers, a sliver of candlelight flickered from beneath the heavy oak door.
He paused.
A muffled sound drifted through the wood. A soft gasp. The unmistakable, rhythmic creak of timber.
Gaelor’s brow furrowed. She should be asleep. He placed a hand on the iron latch. It turned silently. She had forgotten to throw the bolt.
Gaelor pushed the door open.
The world seemed to stop.

On the featherbed, bathed in the soft, orange glow of the hearth, lay his sister, completely naked. And above her, equally bare, was a man sworn to the highest, most sacred vows in the Seven Kingdoms.
For a fraction of a second, no one moved. Then panic shattered the air.
Maela shrieked, scrambling for the tangled bedsheets. "How dare you!" Maela screamed, her face flushed red with rage and shame. "Get out! How dare you enter my chambers!"
Gaelor did not speak. The wine in his veins turned to ice, and then to fire.

He crossed the room in three massive strides. Before Vance could even form the words "My Prince", Gaelor’s fist crashed into the knight’s face. The sickening crunch of cartilage echoed in the room. Vance was thrown backward, his skull rebounding off the stone wall with a hollow crack. He crumpled to the floor, blood pouring in thick, dark ribbons from his shattered nose.
"I heard a noise," Gaelor growled, his voice a low, terrifying rumble. "I thought you were in danger, sister."
He shoved Maela back onto the mattress, his heavy hand pressing against her collarbone. Vance groaned, struggling onto his hands and knees, a pathetic, naked creature bleeding onto the Myrish rug.
"You will say nothing!" Maela spat at Gaelor, her chest heaving, fear finally bleeding through her fury. "Swear to me you will tell no one!"
Gaelor turned his back on her, stepped toward the kneeling knight, and delivered a brutal kick to Vance’s ribs. The knight collapsed, gasping for air.

"Maela," Gaelor said, his voice terrifyingly calm. "Do you want this to reach Father? Do you have any idea what he will do to you? To him?" He pointed a thick finger at the bloody mess on the floor. "You are a Princess of the Blood. He is the Kingsguard. Have you lost your fucking mind?"
"I met the suitors!" Maela yelled back, tears of frustration stinging her eyes. "I hated them! I didn't want them! What am I supposed to do, rot in this tower?"
Gaelor snatched Vance’s white robe from the floor and threw it at the knight’s shivering body. "Put it on."
"Leave him alone, Gaelor!" Maela demanded, trying to stand.
Gaelor shoved her back into the room with brutal force, slamming the inner door shut. "Stay out of this. This man is dead."
"My Prince, please," Vance choked out, spitting blood as he fumbled with the white cloth. "I yielded to weakness. I—"
Gaelor backhanded him across the face, silencing the plea. "On your feet."
He dragged the stumbling knight down the winding, torchlit stairs into the black cells. Two gold cloaks stood at the entrance to the deep dungeons.
He threw Vance into an empty cell, the damp cold of the stone floor biting into the knight's bare flesh. Gaelor ripped the white robe away from him.

"You broke your vows," Gaelor said, drawing the Valyrian steel blade, Blackfyre, from its scabbard. The dark, rippling metal seemed to drink the meager torchlight. He tossed a standard iron arming sword to the stone floor. It clattered loudly. "Fight for your honor."

Vance stared at the sword, then down at his own naked, shivering body. "My Prince... I beg you. Do not do this. I broke my sacred oath. I know my life is forfeit. Let me die with what little honor I have left. Not like this. Not a mummer's farce."
"This is the most honorable death you will ever be offered," Gaelor said, stepping into the cell.

"I cannot draw steel against royal blood," Vance wept, curling his arms over his chest. "I cannot. It was a moment of weakness. It was mutual, my Prince. I swear it. I never thought it would go this far."
Gaelor stepped forward. With a flick of his wrist, he pressed the razor-sharp edge of Blackfyre against Vance’s groin. A thin line of crimson bloomed against the pale skin.
Vance gasped, freezing completely.
"Tell me the truth," Gaelor whispered. "Tell me exactly what happened, or your end will be far slower than a sword through the heart."
"She called me to her room!" Vance sobbed, his eyes wide with absolute terror. "She didn't force me, but she initiated it! It was mutual! Please!"
"Pray to whatever gods you still believe in that it was me who found you, and not my father," Gaelor said coldly, stepping back. "Pick up the sword."
Vance scrambled for the iron hilt. His hands shook so violently the blade rattled. He scrambled backward, bringing the sword up in a pathetic guard.
Gaelor attacked. He did not swing to kill. He swung to humiliate. He delivered shallow, stinging cuts to Vance’s thighs, his arms, his chest. Vance merely dodged, weeping, refusing to strike back.
Finally, driven by the agonizing sting of Valyrian steel, Vance let out a guttural cry and swung hard at the Prince’s head.
Gaelor parried the clumsy strike effortlessly, twisting his wrists to bind Vance's blade. With a brutal, sweeping arc, Gaelor brought Blackfyre down.
The blade sheared cleanly through flesh.
Vance shrieked—a high, inhuman sound—as his severed manhood hit the wet stone. He collapsed, clutching himself, writhing in a pool of his own blood.

Gaelor did not let him scream for long. He stepped over the thrashing knight and drove the dark sword straight down through the back of Vance’s neck, severing the spine. The screaming stopped instantly.
Gaelor pulled the blade free, wiping it on the white cloak discarded in the corner. He looked at the two guards who had rushed down at the sounds of the screaming.
"Get this out of here," Gaelor commanded. Ser Brannyn Vance was no more.
He returned to Maela’s chambers. The princess was pacing like a caged panther.
"What did you do?" she demanded.
"That is my business," Gaelor snapped. "I am the rightful heir to the Iron Throne. I handled it."
Maela let out a bitter, mocking laugh. "You are not the rightful heir. Visenor is. Who in the Seven Hells do you think you are?"

Gaelor’s eyes flashed with fury. "Oh, so now Visenor matters to you? You were perfectly happy whispering poison behind his back with Jace when he was here. Where is your precious brother now? Dead in a ditch in the Marches? Put yourself in my shoes. Any man would have done what I did."
He walked over to the vanity and picked up the steaming cup. "Drink your tea."
Maela snatched the cup and hurled the scalding liquid directly into Gaelor’s face.
Gaelor roared, wiping the hot tea from his eyes. "What is wrong with you?!"
"Get out!" Maela screamed, pointing at the door.

Gaelor stepped into her space, towering over her, his voice a lethal whisper. "Mother and Father are breaking under the weight of this realm. If what you did tonight ever sees the light of day, it will destroy this family. Get a grip, Maela. Do not make this harder than it already is."

He walked to the hearth, poured fresh water from a kettle into a new cup of herbs, and set it on the table. "Drink the tea. I will not force it down your throat. This shitty, pathetic secret stays between us."
Maela stared at him with pure hatred, but her hand trembled as she reached for the cup. She drank it. Gaelor turned and left her to her misery.
The Fourth Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC

The morning air was crisp and smelled of sea salt. Jace woke with a rare, genuine smile touching his lips. He broke his fast with Ser Alester in the solar, enjoying the quiet before the castle woke. Lady Lorenah Dayne was still asleep in the guest chambers.

An hour later, the training yard echoed with the sharp clash of steel. Jace danced backward, parrying a heavy overhead strike from Ser Orwell Morrigen. Sweat beaded on Jace's brow, but his footwork was flawless. Alester leaned against the wooden fence, watching with a critical eye. A few yards away, the young dragon Jhagar gnawed lazily on a charred sheep bone.
Morrigen stepped back, lowering his practice sword. "You grow faster by the day, Ser Jacaelon. Congratulations on your knighthood."
"Thank you, Ser Orwell," Jace panted, wiping his forehead with the back of his glove.
Alester pushed off the fence and walked over. "So, my Prince. Have you decided when we shall hold this tourney?"
Jace handed his training sword to a squire and grabbed a waterskin. "Do not laugh," Jace warned, taking a long drink. "Kingsguard word?"
"Sure, what is it?" Alester said.
"Gaelor should not participate."
Alester frowned. "If the Crown Prince rides, it brings greater prestige to the event."
"The event will have prestige enough," Jace countered flatly. "It would be better if he sat with the King."
"Are you afraid you'll draw him in the tilts?" Alester asked, a knowing glint in his good eye.
"You know as well as I do that he is a better fighter," Jace admitted without shame.
"I knighted you because I saw promise in you," Alester reminded him gently.
"Promise does not stop a lance from shattering my ribs," Jace retorted. "Everyone knows he can unhorse me. Perhaps in the joust I have a slim chance, but you know I despise taking unnecessary risks."
"A true knight embraces the risk, Jace."
Jace shot him a dry look. "And what does a realistic knight do?"
"We are not sharing a bed, my Prince," Alester said, throwing Jace's old banter back at him. "This is a matter of honor."
"Sure. You never share a bed." Jace winked.
Alester replied. "Anyway... Let us not stray from the subject."
"We can stray," Jace said, leaning against the fence. "I assume you slept very well last night after your moonlit stroll with Saera."
Alester sighed. "I merely walked with the Princess. What else would I do?"
"You could do something," Jace teased. "But if you want me to survive this tourney, you need to prepare me properly. Unhorsing Gaelor would please you just as much as me."

"Then make certain you win," Alester said. "Prince Gaelor is fierce, yes. But he is a prince. Half the men he fights let him win. You spar with me day and night. Gaelor's greatest opponent lately was a fifteen-year-old boy."
Jace chuckled, a dark, grim sound. "True enough."
"You ride well," Alester pressed. "Maybe not as well as Prince Gaelor, but jousting is merely a matter of timing and leverage."
"So you admit I am not as good as he is."
"I wasn't as good as six men," Alester pointed out quietly. "But I saw it through."
"You are here precisely because you were as good as six men," Jace corrected.
Alester shook his head. "If we postpone this, when will you face him? This feud between you must end on the field, in the light of day. Lose today, win tomorrow."
"I need to win today, Alester."
"So when does the tourney take place?"
"How much time would I need to be ready for the lists?"
"We start today," Alester declared. "Though it means you will have far less time to entertain Lady Dayne."
"Why?" Jace asked, raising an eyebrow. "Are we training until the moon rises?"
"If we don't, you will never beat him."
"But Lady Lorenah is my guest."
Alester sighed. "I know."

"I cannot tell you how to treat your guests," Alester said softly. "But keeping Gaelor out of his own tourney... that is a defeat before you ever mount a horse. You are starting by losing. Don't you see that?"
Jace stared at the dirt for a long moment. "Fine. If we must break lances until midnight, we will. But there is another problem. Steffon Baratheon is riding as well."
"There will be a dozen men in those lists better than you on paper," Alester said.
"Yes, but two of them harbor a burning desire to see me dead."
Alester crossed his arms. "If you do not wish to ride, let us cancel the mummer's farce."
"We will hold it," Jace said firmly. "I am merely explaining the gravity of the situation. Whatever your commands are, Ser, we begin today."

Jace left the yard to find Lorenah. He found her in the Godswood, trying to converse with little Princess Vhaemys. The young girl was having none of it, huffing and puffing, crossing her arms and glaring at the Dornishwoman.
Saera was sitting on a nearby bench, hiding a laugh behind her hand. When she saw Jace, she waved him over. "Take Vhaemys, Jace. Lady Lorenah and I haven't been able to speak a word."
Jace walked over, offering a polite bow. "Good morning, my ladies."
"I hear you are preparing for the tourney," Lorenah said, her violet eyes sparkling with amusement. "Did you break your fast?"
"I did," Jace said. "I fear the next fortnight will be nothing but sweat and bruised ribs."
Lorenah smiled, entirely understanding. "I would expect nothing less. I should very much want the knight holding my favor to win."
Jace chuckled. "The important thing is participating, is it not?"
Lorenah laughed aloud, a bright, musical sound that made Vhaemys scowl even harder.
Jace scooped the little girl up. "Come along, little terror. Let's go see Jhagar."
As they walked toward the Dragonpit, Vhaemys tugged on Jace's tunic. "Are you going to marry her? Why is she here? You're just doing this to make Father angry, aren't you?"
Jace sighed. "Do not speak so, Vhaemys. Lady Lorenah is our guest, and she is a sweet woman. Once you know her, you will like her. Trust your brother."
Vhaemys blew a raspberry, wriggling out of his arms to run toward the young dragon.
The Eighth Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC
The raven arrived at Starfall bearing the wax seal of the Hand. Maester Edmyn broke it and delivered the news to Prince Visenor: a grand tourney was to be held in King's Landing.
Visenor read the parchment, then fed it to the hearth. It was time. He could not remain a shadow forever.
He found Rhaella in their chambers and kissed her deeply. "I am going back for him. To claim him completely."

He packed his bags with heavier supplies, specifically bringing cuts of salted mutton and fresh goat meat. He knew the path now. He left Roach at the base of the mountains after a day's hard ride and began the brutal ascent. Two days of scaling the jagged shale brought him to the mouth of the blackened cave.
Boneskin heard him coming. A low, vibrating trill echoed from the dark. Two pale, glowing eyes materialized in the shadows.
"Lykirī," Visenor said softly, tossing a leg of mutton onto the stone.

Boneskin crept forward, snapping up the meat. Visenor sat down, eating his own rations. They shared the meal in quiet companionship. When Visenor reached out to touch the beast's snout, Boneskin flinched away.

Visenor closed his eyes and began to sing. The ancient, haunting melodies of Old Valyria drifted through the thin mountain air. Slowly, the tension left the dragon’s coiled muscles. Boneskin lowered his massive head, allowing Visenor to stroke the warm, ivory scales along his crest.

When night fell, wrapping the mountains in total blackness, Visenor took a breath and hoisted himself onto the dragon's back. There was no saddle, no chains, only the hard ridges of the beast's spine.
Boneskin raised his head, letting out a sharp hiss, but he did not leave the cave. The dragon turned his long neck, staring pointedly at the large, scaled egg resting in the back of the cavern.
Visenor understood. He examined the dragon's scales closely in the dim light, looking for the telltale dullness of Ashscale that Baelor had written of, but the beast seemed healthy.
"There is a safer nest in the south," Visenor whispered in High Valyrian. "Let us take your egg. We go together."
Boneskin moved to the back of the cave, delicately grasping the heavy egg in his massive front claws. He crept to the edge of the precipice.
Without warning, the dragon dropped like a stone into the abyss.
Visenor’s stomach leapt into his throat. For three terrifying seconds, they plummeted in freefall. Then, the massive, leathery wings snapped open with a sound like a cracking whip.

They surged upward, tearing through the cloud cover. The night was overcast, but above the clouds, the moon bathed the world in silver. Visenor looked down through breaks in the mist, seeing the pale stone of Starfall, the rushing Torrentine, the entirety of Dorne spread out like a map.
He clung desperately to the dragon's spikes, his knuckles white, the freezing wind whipping through his short, dyed-black hair. He was terrified, but he was alive. He was a dragonrider.

He guided Boneskin south, toward the sea. After an hour of searching the rugged coastline, he spotted the cavern he had marked in his memory days ago. Boneskin banked sharply and landed smoothly on the rocky shore. The waves crashed violently just below the entrance. The cave was deep, damp, and smelled of salt. Safe from men. Safe from everything but scorpions.
Boneskin gently deposited the egg in a hollow of soft sand.
"Your new nest," Visenor whispered.
He left the beast to rest and returned to Starfall as dawn broke over the sea. When he found Rhaella, he held her tight, his heart still hammering with the thrill of the sky.
"I have him," Visenor told her, burying his face in her neck. "And he brought his egg. Our child will have a dragon, Rhaella. I swear it to you."
The Twelfth to the Seventeenth Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC
King's Landing became a swollen beast as the tourney approached. Lords, hedge knights, and sellswords poured through the Mud Gate, erecting a sea of colorful pavilions beneath the city walls.
Prince Gaelor spent his days in the yards, breaking lances and polishing his diplomatic veneer with the arriving lords.
Queen Jaery, watching the court from the balconies, noticed Maela’s deepening melancholy. The princess was hollow-eyed, jumping at sudden noises, refusing to eat.
"You did not care for the Baratheon boy, that is fine," Jaery told her daughter one evening. "But you must meet a lord at this tourney. You cannot wither away in these halls."
"We will see, Mother," Maela said emptily.
"Why are you so joyless?" Jaery pressed.
Maela merely turned away, offering no answer.

Jace, buried in the logistics of the realm and his grueling secret training with Alester, barely saw Lorenah Dayne. On the few nights they managed to share a flagon of wine, Lorenah remained polite, though Jace could sense a quiet disappointment in her violet eyes. She had expected more than stolen hours in the shadows.
King Baelenys remained locked in his solar. He left the endless stream of audiences and the petty squabbles of the smallfolk entirely to the Hand.
When the Master of Laws pressed Gaelor about the execution of Ser Vance, Gaelor lied without blinking. "He was Derrin Hightower’s man. A traitor."
The tourney was set for the eighteenth.
The Seventeenth Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC
"Are you weeping for Ser Vance?" Saera asked, sitting beside Maela in the Godswood. "I know he was your sworn shield, but he worked for the traitor. He would have sold us all."
Maela stared at her hands. "I think he was framed."

Saera tilted her head, her sharp instincts catching the slight tremor in her sister's voice. She did not press, but a cold seed of suspicion took root in her mind. Gaelor had done something terrible, and he was hiding it behind the Hand's purge.
In the armory, Gaelor was pulling off his heavy plate when Ser Saathos entered, his boots caked in fresh mud.
"You return," Gaelor grunted, wiping sweat from his neck. "What did you find at the sept?"

"Not much," Saathos admitted, leaning against a weapon rack. "Had to shake the brothers up a bit to loosen their tongues. It wasn't pretty, but it's done. That night, a blonde knight arrived. Nobody recognized him. He was met by two people already staying at the sept—a man and a woman. They all left together the next morning."
Saathos crossed his arms. "I knew Curtass Whent before he died. I don't know a single knight alive who can take five or six hardened sellswords alone. And since Ser Morrigen never left the city..."
Gaelor frowned. "Is that all?"

"There were no other corpses," Saathos added. "Maybe Whent's men killed the knight's companions, and he fought his way out and fled to the sept. But it doesn't make sense. And the two waiting at the sept... a man and a woman."
Gaelor's mind immediately went to Ser Alester Dayne. But Alester had gone to Dorne to fetch Lady Lorenah. He had returned battered, yes, but fighting six men alone? For what purpose?
"It stinks, my Prince," Saathos said.
"We need to dig into this," Gaelor said, his jaw tight.

"How?" Saathos asked reasonably. "Even if we suspect someone, how many blonde knights are there in King's Landing? Ser Morrigen was here. Alester Dayne wasn't, but he was escorting the Dayne girl. If we start questioning that cover story, it opens a massive can of worms. We'd have to interrogate the Hand. I've never heard of a plot this convoluted."
Gaelor rubbed his temples. "Focus on the tourney for now. We will unearth this rot later."
"As you command," Saathos said. "By the way, your brother is currently in a council meeting."
In the Small Council chambers, Maester Cordin steepled his fingers. "Given the urgency of this matter, perhaps Prince Gaelor should be present?"

"Not necessary," King Baelenys rasped from the head of the table. "The fewer men who know of this, the better." The King turned his heavy gaze to the Grand Maester. "Is this what we discussed a fortnight ago, Baelor?"

"It is, Your Grace," Baelor Targaryen said, adjusting his spectacles. "I have spoken at length with the envoys from Braavos. We made it clear that harboring Vahaemon is an act of war against the Iron Throne. We reminded them that our gold flows into their coffers, and that we honored their trust by executing Derrin Hightower for his treachery. They understood. Vahaemon has been expelled from Braavos."

Baelor leaned forward over the painted map. "The whispers say he sails for Pentos. Your Grace, we are aware you demand the traitor’s head. Braavos was a good step towards our goal, but we need to do the same for Pentos as well."
The King’s cheeks were flushed, his bad eye drooping heavily. "Is this merely political pressure again?" he asked.

"Yes," Baelor confirmed. "Our goal is to funnel him south, toward Tyrosh. We have received new intelligence. The usurper possesses a dragon. How he acquired it, or how long he has had it, we do not know. This complicates matters immensely."

Baelor looked around the table. "We must utilize Princess Saera. We need her dragon. We know her siblings have failed to convince her to fight for the Crown's vanity. But Tyrosh is perfect. They are slavers. We can frame this campaign not as a war for succession, but as a war of liberation. Saera will fight to free slaves. Furthermore, Tyrosh is closer, and requires less gold to besiege. If the Archon protects Vahaemon, we burn their fleets. If they hand him over, the war ends in a day."
Lord Tion Lannister frowned. "Will Pentos truly bow so easily?"
"If Braavos bent the knee," the King said dismissively, "Pentos will not dare cross us." The King looked to his Hand.
Jace leaned back in his chair. "Uncle Baelor has worked tirelessly on this, and the logic is sound. But..."
"We cannot go to war against a dragon without ensuring the victory in advance," Baelor insisted.
"Will Saera truly be convinced?" the King asked, skeptical. "We are using slaves as a mummer's trick."
"Jace and I will handle Saera," Baelor assured him.
Jace’s violet eyes were hard. "I am not thinking about convincing her. I am thinking about risking my sister's life against an unknown dragon."
The King scoffed. "Did she not always say she wanted to die for the peasants?"
Jace met his father's gaze without flinching. "Did you not always tell her that was incredibly stupid?"
Baelor held up a hand to keep the peace. "We do not intend to throw her into the vanguard. But two dragons are vastly superior to one."

Jace leaned forward, placing his hands flat on the table. "We played the game well in Braavos. We can repeat it in Pentos, and they will yield, just as Father says. We will do what must be done with Tyrosh. But why this desperate rush to war? Vahaemon knows we have at least two fully grown dragons. He is not going to attack King's Landing. Meanwhile, we have fresh dragons training in the pit. If we wait a few years, we will be untouchable. Why not pivot to something profitable, like the Stepstones, while we starve him of allies?"
Maester Cordin saw his chance to flatter the King. "The King's primary concern in this matter—"
Jace cut him off with a single, sharp look, turning immediately back to Baelor.
"The King's primary concern in this matter," Baelor said smoothly, seamlessly picking up the thread, "is that Vahaemon will sire children."

The King slammed his fist onto the table. "The realm is shaken! Having a claimant out there, breathing, breathing free, gives power to every dissident lord in the Seven Kingdoms. He was a popular man once. The current unrest gives him strength. There cannot be a duality in House Targaryen. He is not the rightful heir, yet he draws support. It is an insult to the Crown’s prestige. Furthermore, he possesses artifacts of our house—swords, crowns, texts—that belong in this keep. They will be returned."
Jace stared at the map. The King was ruled by pride and paranoia. There was no arguing with a man who fought ghosts.
The council was dismissed.

The noise of the encamped tourney participants drifted over the walls of the Red Keep. Jace was restless, pacing the training yard. His paranoia was a living thing. Tomorrow, he would ride in the lists. Gaelor would be there. Lorenah would be watching.
He saw Gaelor practicing at the quintain, his lance shattering a heavy oak shield with brutal force.
Jace walked past the fence. "Train well, brother. You will need it."
Gaelor tossed the splintered lance aside and laughed. "Of course, Jace. Try not to fall off your horse before we meet."
Jace continued toward the stables, looking for Alester. Instead, he found Lord Steffon Baratheon dismounting his massive destrier.
Steffon handed the reins to a squire and turned, his chest puffed out. "Prince Jacaelon."
"Lord Steffon," Jace said, his voice a mask of polite indifference. "You honor us with your presence."
"I hear you are riding in the lists tomorrow. I hope we have the chance to meet on the field," Steffon said.
"I cannot say I hope for it as much as you do, my Lord."

Steffon let out a booming laugh, resting his hands on his thick belt. He looked around the yard. "It seems half the realm has answered the call. Only Lord Rickard remains in the North, still nursing his grief."
"We mourn with him," Jace said dryly.
"Until tomorrow, then," Steffon said, his eyes raking over Jace’s slighter frame with visible contempt before he marched toward the keep.
Jace finally found Alester instructing a stableboy on the proper care of a destrier's barding.
"Are you nervous?" Alester asked quietly as Jace approached.
"A bit."
"You are as prepared as you can be."
"We will see."

Alester clapped him on the shoulder. "Before every tourney, I do myself a favor. I go and drink until I forget the smell of horse shit. I am going down to Flea Bottom. The air is better there than among these snobs strutting around in armor painted with stags and birds. Will you come?"
Jace smiled. "A fine idea. Let us go."

When night fell, they donned their ragged cloaks, concealing their silver hair, and slipped out of the Red Keep. They wound their way into the labyrinth of Flea Bottom, ducking into a familiar, dimly lit tavern that smelled of roasted pork and stale ale.

They found a table in the corner. Jace drank deeply, the tension of the coming day slowly bleeding out of his shoulders. He downed six tankards of dark ale in rapid succession. Alester kept pace, but tapped out at five.
"You win the cup," Alester laughed, wiping foam from his mouth. "I hope you ride half as well as you drink tomorrow."

Across the tavern, a group of young women noticed Alester’s handsome, albeit bruised, face. They giggled, making eyes at him. Alester noticed, offering a charming smile, but he hesitated, glancing at Jace.
"What happened to your sacred vows?" Jace teased, taking another long swallow of ale.
"I haven't done anything," Alester defended himself.
"You thought about it."
"What is the harm in looking?"

The girls gathered courage and approached the table, leaning in close, pouring ale and fawning over the knight. Alester engaged them in easy, laughing conversation, making no moves to bed them, simply enjoying the attention.
Jace turned his back to the crowd, resting his elbows on the sticky wood of the table.

At the far end of the tavern, sitting alone in the shadows, was a woman. She had raven-black hair pulled back beneath a dark hood. But it wasn't her hair that caught Jace's attention. It was the thick cloth tied securely over her eyes. She was blind.

Yet, her head was turned directly toward Jace. And it stayed that way. For six, then seven minutes, every time Jace glanced over, the blind woman was "staring" exactly at him. Beside her boots rested a long, heavy bag wrapped in canvas.
Curiosity overrode caution. Jace picked up his half-empty tankard and walked through the noisy crowd, pulling out the chair opposite her.
"You come to a lady's table and you do not bring her an ale?" the woman asked. Her voice was smooth, cultured, entirely out of place in Flea Bottom.
"I brought mine," Jace said, sliding the tankard across the wood.
The woman reached out with unerring precision, took the tankard, and took a sip. She leaned forward over the table.
"I would like to know you better," she said softly. "If I may."
She reached her hand across the table, aiming directly for his face. Jace glanced back at Alester, who was completely engrossed in a story with the tavern girls, oblivious.
"Do not let your friend drink too much," the woman murmured.

Her fingers found Jace’s cheek. Her touch was calloused, the hands of a swordswoman, not a lady. She traced his jawline, her fingers slipping up into the coarse hood to touch the silver-gold strands of his hair. Her thumb brushed lightly over his eyelid.
"A Prince," she whispered, a smirk playing on her lips. "Here. At this hour."
Jace stiffened, his drunken haze vanishing instantly. "Do we know each other?"
"Perhaps you do not remember me," she said, leaning back. "Because you are a prince, and princes have much to occupy their minds."
"Where should I remember you from?" Jace asked, his hand slipping beneath his cloak to rest on the hilt of his dagger. Is she a woods witch? A shadowbinder?

The woman took another sip of his ale, ignoring the question. "I have heard a rumor," she said, her voice dropping to a husky purr. "I heard that a Targaryen prince fucks better than any man in the Seven Kingdoms. Are you him, or is it the other Prince?"
"There aren't two princes," Jace said carefully.
"Then it is not you."
"Wouldn't you like to find out?" Jace countered, his pride flaring.

The woman smiled, revealing perfectly white teeth. "Perhaps. But I do not know you. Are you Prince Jacaelon, or Prince Gaelor? Though, I suppose if you were the other one, you would not be sitting in a tavern in Flea Bottom."
Jace's mind raced. She thinks I am Gaelor. "You said it yourself," Jace laughed, playing along.
"I have things I could show you," the woman said, standing up and grabbing the heavy canvas bag from the floor. "But yes. I would like to find out."

She turned toward the stairs leading to the brothel rooms above. Jace stood. He glanced at Alester, who was raising a cup to the cheering girls, and followed the blind woman up the creaking wooden steps.
She kicked open the door to a small, damp room. Inside, two rough-looking men were sharing a bed with a bruised whore.

Jace stepped out from behind the woman, and waved his hand dismissively. The men, recognizing the bearing and blood of high nobility, grabbed their breeches and scrambled out of the room without a word of protest.
The woman closed the door and dropped the heavy bag onto the floor with a metallic thud. She walked to the bed, gently pushing Jace down onto the mattress. She sat astride his hips.
"Let's see how a Targaryen prince fucks," she whispered.

She pulled her tunic over her head. Her body was magnificent, honed by years of riding and fighting, her skin pale in the moonlight filtering through the shutters. She reached for a half-empty flagon of wine left by the previous occupants and took a long drink while she rode him.
She pulled the flagon away, grimacing in disgust, and handed it down to Jace. "I do not like the wine here. You people in the capital do not know how to make wine."
Jace took a sip, the sour vintage burning his throat. "Where should we drink wine from, then?"
"Dorne," she said simply.
As she reached down to place the flagon on the floorboards, there was a sharp shing of sliding steel.
Before Jace could react, cold metal pressed firmly against his Adam's apple.
"The rumors were true," she whispered, leaning down so her breath tickled his ear. "You are still rock hard."

Jace froze, his eyes crossing to look at the blade at his throat. The steel was dark, rippling with ancient magic. He recognized it instantly. It was Dark Sister, the ancestral sword of House Targaryen, stolen away by his uncle Vahaemon years ago.
The woman reached up with her free hand and pulled the blindfold from her eyes.
She wasn't blind.
Her eyes were a brilliant, striking purple.
"We finally meet, cousin," she smiled.

title: Chapter IX: The Brothers' Tilt
synopsis: A perilous encounter in a Flea Bottom brothel leaves Prince Jacaelon shaken, while a grand tourney in King's Landing brings long-simmering rivalries to a brutal, bloody climax in the lists.
content: The Seventeenth Day of the Seventh Moon, Ninety-Nine AC
Dark Sister was freezing against his throat.

The Valyrian steel bit just enough to draw a bead of warm blood, a sharp contrast to the heat of the hips grinding down against his own. Jace’s breath hitched, trapped somewhere between his chest and the rippled steel pressing into his windpipe. The bedropes groaned rhythmically beneath them in the dark, the scent of sweat and wine heavy in the air.
He stared up into the woman’s face. The moonlight filtering through the shutters caught on a jagged scar that cut across her cheek, but it was her unblinking amethyst eyes that held him pinned.
She rode him slow, agonizingly deliberate, her arm fully extended to keep the ancestral blade resting against his carotid artery. She thought he was Gaelor. He knew that much.
